# Getting started {#sec-getting-started}

This chapter explains how to open the CARS data in a spreadsheet and in code.

## In a spreadsheet

The aggregate tables are ordinary CSV files and open directly in Excel,
LibreOffice Calc, Google Sheets or Numbers.

- **Size.** Most tables are well under Excel's limit of 1,048,576 rows. The
  largest, such as `mileage_by_pca_year_body_fuel.csv`, are several megabytes
  and open fine, but are easier to work with through a PivotTable.
- **Opening a CSV in Excel.** Double-clicking a CSV works, but Excel may
  change values it thinks are dates or numbers. For full control use **Data ›
  From Text/CSV** and check the column types in the preview.
- **Postcode area codes.** Codes are one or two letters (`B`, `LS`). Excel
  will not change them, but take care with codes such as `NA` that some tools
  read as missing; no real postcode area uses it.
- **PivotTables** (Insert › PivotTable) are the main tool for the examples
  in @sec-examples-spreadsheet: they filter, group and sum the long tables.

::: {.callout-tip title="Excel tables"}
Converting the data to an Excel table (select a cell, then Ctrl+T) makes
filtering easier and lets formulas refer to columns by name.
:::

## In code: DuckDB

The vehicle table is too large for a spreadsheet, and too large to load into
memory in most tools, but [DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/) can query it in place.
DuckDB is a free, fast database that runs inside R, Python or on its own, with
no server to set up. It reads only the columns a query needs, so most queries
on the vehicle table take seconds on an ordinary laptop.

The examples in this book are written in DuckDB's SQL, so they work the same
from any language. Each refers to the file as `vehicles_enhanced.parquet`;
replace that with the path to your copy.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## R

```r
install.packages("duckdb")

library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())

dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT fuel_simple, count(*) AS n_vehicles
  FROM read_parquet('vehicles_enhanced.parquet')
  GROUP BY fuel_simple
  ORDER BY n_vehicles DESC
")

dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

Packages such as `dplyr` (with `duckplyr` or `dbplyr`) and `arrow` can also
query the file without writing SQL.

## Python

```python
# pip install duckdb
import duckdb

duckdb.sql("""
  SELECT fuel_simple, count(*) AS n_vehicles
  FROM read_parquet('vehicles_enhanced.parquet')
  GROUP BY fuel_simple
  ORDER BY n_vehicles DESC
""").df()
```

`polars` and `pandas` (with `pyarrow`) can also read the file, but pandas
loads everything into memory, so read only the columns you need.

## Command line

```sh
# Install from https://duckdb.org/docs/installation/
duckdb -c "
  SELECT fuel_simple, count(*) AS n_vehicles
  FROM read_parquet('vehicles_enhanced.parquet')
  GROUP BY fuel_simple
  ORDER BY n_vehicles DESC"
```

:::

### Practical advice

- **Look before you query.** `DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM
  read_parquet('vehicles_enhanced.parquet')` lists the columns and their types
  instantly.
- **Select only the columns you need.** `SELECT *` on the full table reads all
  of it. Name columns, or use DuckDB's `COLUMNS('^pca_')` to pick a set by
  pattern.
- **Aggregate in DuckDB and bring back the result.** Bring a summary into R or
  Python, not 93 million rows.
- **Memory.** DuckDB uses up to 80% of memory by default and spills to disk
  when it needs more. For reshaping the whole table into long form, give it
  plenty of disk space (`SET temp_directory = '...'`), or work on a subset.
- **Try ideas on a subset.** Filter to one make, one area or a random sample
  (`USING SAMPLE 1%`) while developing a query, then run it on everything.

## Hardware

Any recent laptop with 8 GB of memory and space for the 9 GB file can run the
examples in this book. Reshaping the full table into one row per vehicle per
year (about 2 billion rows) is better done on a machine with 32 GB or more,
or broken into pieces.
